title: Man's Search for Meaning
subtitle: Viktor Frankl
description: Frankl's account of surviving Nazi concentration camps and the psychotherapeutic approach (logotherapy) he developed from it, arguing that finding meaning is what sustains people through unavoidable suffering.

title: Nicomachean Ethics
subtitle: Aristotle
description: The foundational text of virtue ethics, arguing that character is built through repeated practice of virtuous action until it becomes habitual, and that virtue typically lies as a mean between two extremes.

title: Meditations
subtitle: Marcus Aurelius
description: The private notebook of a Roman emperor practicing Stoic philosophy, focused on self-discipline, duty, and maintaining equanimity regardless of circumstance.

title: Atomic Habits
subtitle: James Clear
description: A practical synthesis of habit-formation research showing how small, consistent behavioral changes compound over time, and why identity ('the kind of person who...') drives discipline more reliably than willpower alone.

title: Grit: The Power of Passion and Perseverance
subtitle: Angela Duckworth
description: Duckworth's research-based case that sustained effort toward long-term goals ('grit') predicts achievement better than talent alone, drawing on her studies of West Point cadets, spelling-bee competitors, and others.

title: The Power of Habit
subtitle: Charles Duhigg
description: An accessible explanation of the cue-routine-reward habit loop and how identifying 'keystone habits' can be used to deliberately reshape behavior.

title: Mindset: The New Psychology of Success
subtitle: Carol Dweck
description: Dweck's research distinguishing a 'fixed' mindset, which treats ability as static, from a 'growth' mindset, which treats it as developed through effort—directly relevant to how people respond to setbacks and failure.

title: Thanks!: How the New Science of Gratitude Can Make You Happier
subtitle: Robert Emmons
description: Emmons summarizes his own experimental research on gratitude practices, presenting evidence for their measurable effects on well-being rather than treating gratitude as merely a nice sentiment.

title: The Road to Character
subtitle: David Brooks
description: Brooks contrasts 'resume virtues' (achievements) with 'eulogy virtues' (humility, honesty, courage), profiling historical figures who built the latter through struggle and self-examination.

title: Extreme Ownership
subtitle: Jocko Willink and Leif Babin
description: Two former Navy SEAL officers argue, from their own combat leadership experience, that taking full responsibility for outcomes—rather than assigning blame—is the basis of both discipline and effective leadership.

title: Angela Duckworth
subtitle: Psychologist, University of Pennsylvania
description: Beyond her original grit research, Duckworth founded Character Lab, a nonprofit that develops and tests practical tools for building character strengths in students.

title: Carol Dweck
subtitle: Psychologist, Stanford University
description: Dweck's growth-mindset research began with studies of how children respond differently to failure and praise, work that has since been extended (and debated) across education and organizational settings.

title: Robert Emmons
subtitle: Psychologist, UC Davis; gratitude researcher
description: Emmons is among the field's founding researchers on gratitude as a measurable psychological variable and edits the Journal of Positive Psychology, one of the discipline's core academic outlets.

title: Viktor Frankl
subtitle: Neurologist, psychiatrist, and Holocaust survivor
description: Frankl developed logotherapy, sometimes called the 'Third Viennese School of Psychotherapy' after Freud's and Adler's, centered on the search for meaning as a primary human motivation.

title: Brené Brown
subtitle: Research professor, University of Houston
description: Brown's qualitative research on vulnerability, shame, and courage argues that the willingness to be seen as imperfect is a precondition for genuine connection and resilience, not a weakness to be hidden.

title: Positive Psychology and Character Strengths
description: Founded by Martin Seligman, this field studies what enables people to flourish rather than only what goes wrong; Christopher Peterson and Seligman's VIA classification catalogs widely recognized character strengths across cultures.

title: Moral Psychology
description: Research on how people actually reason about right and wrong, including Jonathan Haidt's moral foundations theory, which argues moral judgment is driven more by fast intuition than by deliberate reasoning.

title: Self-Control and Delayed Gratification
description: Walter Mischel's marshmallow studies linked children's ability to delay gratification to later life outcomes; later replication attempts found the effect is real but smaller and more dependent on socioeconomic context than the original studies suggested.

title: Post-Traumatic Growth
description: Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun's research area documents how some people report genuine positive psychological change—not just recovery—after struggling with highly challenging life events.

title: Habit Formation Timelines
description: A 2010 study by Phillippa Lally and colleagues tracked how long it actually takes a new behavior to become automatic, finding an average of about 66 days with wide individual variation—directly countering the popular but unsupported '21 days' claim.
